I am sitting in an imaginary room constructed entirely of possibilities, the walls made of shifting sentences and sentences made of bright, holographic letters that rearrange themselves the moment I think I have understood them. A clock without hands hums overhead, punctuating the air with silent ticks that only memory can hear, and on the floor a rug of forgotten metaphors waits for someone brave enough to stand upon it and listen for echoes. Outside, beyond an ajar window, daylight folds into dusk like paper turning itself into origami swans that glide across invisible currents. Their wings whisper of yet-unwritten dreams tonight.

In this interior weather, ideas fall like rain that evaporates before touching the ground, leaving behind only resonant humidity. I gather droplets in cupped palms, watching reflections of places I have never visited ripple across miniature oceans. A lighthouse the size of a thimble appears on one puddle’s horizon, its beam sweeping for lost sentences that wandered too far from their parent paragraph. I want to rescue them, but every time I reach, my elbow brushes against the possibility of distraction, and the image scatters into concentric circles of maybe. Still, I keep collecting, believing concentration can summon continents tomorrow.

I remember reading that imagination is a muscle hidden between the ribs and the lungs, flexed each time we exhale uncertainty. Whether or not the anatomy books confirm this is irrelevant; the sensation remains, a pleasant ache radiating outward whenever language leaps the fence of the expected. Today that muscle twitches at random intervals, like a caught fish refusing to surrender its silver cadence. I lean back, let the spasm write its own rhythm across my sternum, and consider the possibility that stories are small cardiac events—palpitations reminding us we are alive, vulnerable, and urgently unfinished in the half-lit dusk.

Outside the narrative window I built earlier, the swans have multiplied into a constellation of paper birds, each flapping just enough to stay suspended between conviction and collapse. Their shadows, projected on the carpet of forgotten metaphors, resemble hieroglyphs describing a civilization that honors uncertainty as sacred text. I kneel to interpret them, but the lexicon changes whenever I blink, as though meaning itself prefers to dance rather than stand still. It occurs to me that maybe understanding is less a destination than a choreography, and we, the awkward students, keep stepping on our own feet, laughing anyway through everything.

A small radio I hadn’t noticed before crackles from a corner, tuned to a station broadcasting questions instead of music. The voice asks, ‘What color is nostalgia when viewed by tomorrow’s eyes?’ then fades into static. I consider answering aloud, but the silence afterward feels like an invitation to listen rather than speak, so I let the query hang like a lantern whose flame is sound. In that hush, old photographs parade across the walls, each image dissolving before I can recognize faces, leaving only outlines traced in phosphorescent chalk. The absence, surprisingly, feels companionable, a shared invisibility between heartbeats.

Time, sensing my distraction, rearranges itself into a spiral staircase that leads simultaneously upward and inward. I place a tentative foot on the first step and feel stories stored in the grain of the wood vibrate beneath my heel. Each riser hums a note, together forming a scale I almost recognize from childhood humming, but not quite. As I climb, objects from earlier scenes drift past: the thimble lighthouse, a handful of concentric maybes, a silver-scaled fish still twitching with narrative electricity. They orbit me like moons consulting their planet, asking whether gravity or gratitude should guide them tonight onwards.

Near the top—or is it the center?—of the staircase, I encounter a door made entirely of questions left unanswered at dinner tables. Its surface shivers with polite laughter, awkward pauses, abrupt subject changes. To open it, I must select one question and breathe life into it. I choose the simplest: ‘Where have you been?’ The door swings away, revealing an orchard of clocks growing on gnarled trees, each timepiece ripening at its own pace. Some hours are bruised, some minutes freshly blossomed. I pluck a second, hold it to my ear, and hear my grandmother humming lullabies in reverse softly.

The reversed melody unspools memories like film running backward, laughter re-entering mouths, tears retreating into eyes, farewells unsaid becoming greetings not yet spoken. I follow the tune until I arrive at a clearing where sentences stand upright like saplings, eager for sunlight. I run my fingertips along their bark, feeling verbs pulse beneath the surface, sap of potentiality rising. One sentence leans toward me, shadow stretching across my shoes. It whispers, ‘Read me aloud and I will become a road.’ Obligingly, I speak its syllables, and the ground rearranges, forming a path paved with punctuation marks glinting like pebbles underfoot.

I walk the road of spoken possibility, commas obligingly pausing under my steps, semicolons winking conspiratorially. The path curves through fields of unwritten afternoons where sunlight feels like anticipation more than warmth. At the horizon stands a tower built from books I never finished reading; their spines form a mosaic of abandoned intentions. I wonder what stories grew lonely inside those pages, waiting for eyes that never arrived. Guilt and wonder mingle, but neither outweighs the thrill of discovery, so I climb again, this time on stairs bound with ribboned bookmarks, each one fluttering like a reconciled regret at dawn.

From the tower’s summit I can finally see the imaginary room where everything began, its roof now shimmering like a mirage because distance has made it mythic. The paper swans orbit it like satellites of creative yearning, and the clocks in their orchard chime asynchronously, composing a symphony that somehow fits together. I inhale the thin air of altitude and find it flavored with beginnings. Dropping a pebble of punctuation over the edge, I watch as gravity writes its final line across the sky: not an ending, merely a turning page. I smile, tuck the view into memory, and descend.
